nameStory: Common sea-lavender gets its name from its delicate purple-blue flowers that bloom in airy clusters, reminiscent of the fragrant herb lavender. However, despite the name similarity, this coastal plant isn't actually related to true lavender and doesn't share that distinctive scent. The 'sea' part of its name hints at its true home – the salty marshes and shores where it thrives.
description: Common sea-lavender is a tough, clumping perennial plant that makes its home in New England's salt marshes and coastal areas. It forms neat rosettes of leathery leaves close to the ground, sending up branched flowering stems that can reach 1-2 feet tall. In late summer, it produces clouds of tiny purple-blue flowers that create a misty, ethereal appearance across the marsh landscape. This hardy plant has adapted perfectly to life in salty conditions where few other flowering plants can survive.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, leathery leaves arranged in a basal rosette that feel waxy to the touch, with smooth edges and a paddle-like shape that helps them conserve water in salty conditions

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny purple-blue flowers clustered in airy, branched sprays that feel papery and dry, creating a cloud-like appearance that persists even after drying

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms distinct clumps or colonies with leaves hugging the ground and flower stalks rising 1-2 feet above, creating scattered patches across the marsh

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, repeatedly branched flowering stems that feel firm and somewhat woody, often with a slight reddish tinge

habitat: Look for common sea-lavender in salt marshes, tidal flats, and other coastal areas where salt spray and periodic flooding create challenging growing conditions. In New England, it's found along the Atlantic coast in areas with salty or brackish water, often growing alongside salt marsh asters and glasswort. It prefers areas that flood occasionally with salt water but aren't permanently submerged.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the basal rosette, appearing thick and waxy as they unfurl from the center of established clumps.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in late summer, when the distinctive purple-blue flower clusters create misty clouds above the marsh landscape.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade but often persist as papery, dried clusters that remain attractive and help with identification even after blooming ends.
seasonality.winter: The sturdy basal leaves often remain evergreen in milder areas, while dried flower stems may persist above the marsh as weathered skeletons.

funFact: Common sea-lavender is actually a salt-secreting plant – it actively pumps salt out through special glands on its leaves, sometimes forming tiny white salt crystals on the leaf surface that you can actually taste if you lick them!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Carolina sea-lavender, which is more widespread in New England salt marshes. Carolina sea-lavender tends to have more numerous, smaller flower clusters and slightly narrower leaves, while common sea-lavender has fewer but larger flower branches.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, common sea-lavender is not related to culinary lavender and doesn't share its pleasant fragrance. The name comes purely from the similar purple-blue flower color. In New England, this European native has been introduced and is much less common than the native Carolina sea-lavender.
compareHints: Common sea-lavender differs from Carolina sea-lavender by having fewer but more robust flowering branches and slightly broader leaves. While Carolina sea-lavender creates dense, intricate flower clusters, common sea-lavender tends to have a more open, less densely packed flower arrangement. Both share the same habitat preferences and blooming time, making location and subtle structural differences key to telling them apart.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Carolina Sea Lavender can be distinguished from the non-native Blue Statice by its exclusively coastal habitat and smaller, more delicate flowers – Blue Statice is typically found in gardens and has showier, more colorful blooms.
Blue statice differs from its native New England relatives Carolina sea lavender and common sea-lavender by its much more colorful, ornamental flowers and cultivated garden habitat.
